
This short example shows how to use `drMultiOutITR` with the publicly
available **right-heart catheterization (RHC)** dataset. The example compares
`No RHC` and `RHC` using two responses: **hospital length of stay** and
**survival at 30, 90, and 150 days**. If you are new to the package, start with
the [three-treatment mixed-outcome tutorial](getting-started.html).

The data are available from the
[Vanderbilt University Department of Biostatistics](https://hbiostat.org/data/),
with the [RHC variable description](https://hbiostat.org/data/repo/rhc).
The original study is Connors et al. (1996), *The effectiveness of right heart
catheterization in the initial care of critically ill patients*, JAMA,
276:889–897. Please acknowledge the study and the Vanderbilt data source when
using the dataset.

## Step 1. Install the package

```{r installation, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(c("remotes", "ranger", "survival", "knitr", "rmarkdown"))
# The optional randomForestSRC package is also needed for this RHC example.
# Install a version compatible with your R version.
remotes::install_github("cksiri/drMultiOutITR", build_vignettes = TRUE)
library(drMultiOutITR)
```

## Step 2. Download and prepare the RHC data

The public CSV has 5,735 records. The example follows the outcome construction
and primary 48-covariate specification used in the RHC research workflow,
excluding one record with a missing discharge date. The resulting analysis
sample has **5,734 records**. Preparation is handled by a small script included
with the package; no separate research files are required.

```{r prepare, eval=FALSE}
example_file <- system.file("examples", "rhc_public_data.R",
                            package = "drMultiOutITR")
source(example_file)

csv_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
download.file("https://hbiostat.org/data/repo/rhc.csv",
              destfile = csv_file, mode = "wb")
rhc <- prepare_rhc_public_data(csv_file)
unlink(csv_file)

nrow(rhc$data)           # 5734
length(rhc$covariates)   # 48
table(rhc$data$A_label)
```

If your R session cannot download the CSV automatically, download it manually
from the [Vanderbilt data page](https://hbiostat.org/data/), then pass the
saved file path to `prepare_rhc_public_data("path/to/rhc.csv")`.

## Step 3. Fit a small example and predict treatment rankings

For convenience, the script also provides a one-call demonstration. It draws
**1,600 training records** and **60 held-out records**, fits forests with
**60 trees**, and prints treatment recommendation counts under three outcome
weighting schemes. It does not repeat the original five-fold analysis.

```{r run-example, eval=FALSE}
# With Internet access, the function downloads the public CSV itself.
rhc_example <- run_rhc_public_example()

# Or, if you have already saved the public file:
# rhc_example <- run_rhc_public_example(csv_file = "path/to/rhc.csv")

rhc_example$counts
```

The three schemes are equal weights (`0.5`, `0.5`), length-of-stay-heavy
(`0.7`, `0.3`), and survival-heavy (`0.3`, `0.7`). The model is fitted **once**;
only the weights supplied to `predict()` change. The function returns the fitted
model and aggregate recommendation counts without writing patient-level data or
model files to disk.

## Step 4. Apply the same procedure to your own data

Define pretreatment covariates, the treatment column, continuous quantile
summaries, and survival horizons. Fit with `fit_dr_itr()` and call `predict()`
with new covariate profiles. The [getting-started tutorial](getting-started.html)
shows the complete fit/predict interface with three treatments and three
outcome types.

**About this example:** The small training sample and tree counts are intended
to demonstrate package usage. The published RHC study analysis used a more
extensive held-out procedure; the numbers from this illustration should not be
presented as a reproduction of that analysis.

For the framework, estimation methods, and associated conditions, see
Siriwardhana, Gunaratnam, and Kulasekera (2026),
[*A flexible rank-based framework for individualized treatment selection with
mixed-type multivariate outcomes*](https://doi.org/10.1177/09622802261454791),
and the observational-study extension,
*Doubly Robust Rank-Based Individualized Treatment Selection in Observational
Studies: A Flexible Framework for Mixed-Type Multivariate Outcomes* (manuscript).
